payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through 2025 and structural reasoning. US housing starts (SAAR) ran roughly 1.25–1.45M through 2024–2025, with single-family starts soft (~0.85–0.95M) amid elevated mortgage rates and builder inventory, and multifamily highly volatile month to month. Permits drifted toward ~1.3M in late 2025, suggesting the underlying trend of starts sits close to the 1.30M threshold. A 1.300M strike therefore looks near the center of the plausible September 2026 distribution; monthly noise (typical revisions/standard errors of ±8–10%) dominates any trend signal I can infer without 2026 observations. Too high risk: if 2026 brought continued single-family weakness, tariff-driven cost pressure, or a soft labor market, the trend could have slipped to ~1.20–1.28M, making an above-1.30M print less than even odds; September also sometimes shows seasonal-adjustment quirks and hurricane disruptions in the South. Too low risk: if the Fed eased meaningfully in 2026 and mortgage rates fell toward 6% or below, builder activity and multifamily starts could have rebounded, pushing typical readings to 1.35–1.45M, in which case YES would be clearly favored. Given no evidence on 2026 conditions, I center near 50%. Note the first-print (not revised) value governs, and 'above 1.300M' means strictly greater, though a print exactly at 1.300M is unlikely.
limitations: No 2026 housing, permits, rate, or macro data supplied; estimate relies on pre-2026 background knowledge.
Monthly housing starts are noisy with large sampling error and frequent revisions; first print governs.
Unknown whether the contract ladder strike is centered on current expectations.
Possible delays or data disruptions (e.g., shutdowns, hurricanes) not assessable.
